claim: Sticks and Stones (Sns) is an immunoglobulin superfamily cell adhesion molecule that binds to the Drosophila Type IIa RPTP Lar.
source: We identified the immunoglobulin superfamily CAM Sticks and Stones (Sns) as a new partner for the Drosophila Type IIa RPTP Lar.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that Sns was identified as a new partner for Lar, and this is supported by binding experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lar and Sns bind to each other in embryos.
source: Lar and Sns bind to each other in embryos and in vitro, and the human Sns ortholog, Nephrin, binds to human Type IIa RPTPs.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figure 1 shows embryo staining experiments demonstrating binding.

claim: Lar and Sns bind to each other in vitro.
source: Lar and Sns bind to each other in embryos and in vitro, and the human Sns ortholog, Nephrin, binds to human Type IIa RPTPs.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figure 1P-Q shows ECIA assay results demonstrating in vitro binding.

claim: The human Sns ortholog, Nephrin, binds to human Type IIa RPTPs.
source: Lar and Sns bind to each other in embryos and in vitro, and the human Sns ortholog, Nephrin, binds to human Type IIa RPTPs.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figure 1I-Q shows binding experiments with human proteins.

claim: Lar and Sns function together to regulate larval neuromuscular junction development.
source: Genetic analysis shows that Lar and Sns function together to regulate larval neuromuscular junction development, axon guidance in the mushroom body (MB), and innervation of the optic lobe (OL) medulla by R7 photoreceptors.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figures 2-3 show expression patterns and NMJ phenotypes in Lar/Sns transheterozygotes.

claim: Lar and Sns function together to regulate axon guidance in the mushroom body (MB).
source: Genetic analysis shows that Lar and Sns function together to regulate larval neuromuscular junction development, axon guidance in the mushroom body (MB), and innervation of the optic lobe (OL) medulla by R7 photoreceptors.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figures 4-6 show MB phenotypes in Lar/Sns transheterozygotes.

claim: Lar and Sns function together to regulate innervation of the optic lobe (OL) medulla by R7 photoreceptors.
source: Genetic analysis shows that Lar and Sns function together to regulate larval neuromuscular junction development, axon guidance in the mushroom body (MB), and innervation of the optic lobe (OL) medulla by R7 photoreceptors.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figures 7-8 show expression patterns and R7 targeting phenotypes.

claim: In the neuromuscular system, Lar and Sns are both required in motor neurons and may function as coreceptors.
source: In the neuromuscular system, Lar and Sns are both required in motor neurons, and may function as coreceptors.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figure 2 shows expression in motor neurons, while Figure 3 shows NMJ phenotypes with neuronal RNAi.

claim: In the MB and OL, the relevant Lar-Sns interactions are in trans (between neurons), so Sns functions as a Lar ligand in these systems.
source: In the MB and OL, however, the relevant Lar-Sns interactions are in trans (between neurons), so Sns functions as a Lar ligand in these systems.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, and Figures 4-7 show differential expression patterns supporting trans interactions.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sns in embryos confers binding to the Lar ECD.
source: However, it brightly stained both the CNS axon ladder and the periphery in embryos from a cross between Tub-GAL4 and a line that has an insertion of an EP-like element ~200 bp 5′ to the transcription start of sns (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows bright staining with Lar-AP in Tub>Sns embryos compared to wild-type (Figure 1A).

claim: Lar-AP staining intensity in the periphery increased more than 10-fold in Tub>Sns embryos versus wild-type.
source: Quantification of Lar-AP staining intensity in the periphery showed more than a 10-fold increase in Lar-AP staining in Tub>Sns embryos vs. WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this quantification result, which is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of Lar in embryos increases Sns-AP5 staining three-fold in the CNS compared to wild-type.
source: Embryos with ectopic expression of Lar driven by Tub-GAL4 showed a three-fold increase in Sns-AP5 staining in the CNS compared to WT control embryos (Figure 1D' and H).
evidence: The text states this quantification result, which is shown in Figure 1H.

claim: 60-mer Lar particles exhibit a seven-fold increase in binding to Sns-AP5 bait in ECIA assays.
source: 60-mer Lar 'prey' exhibited a seven-fold increase in binding to Sns-AP5 'bait' coupled to the surface of an ELISA plate, showing that the two proteins interact directly in vitro.
evidence: The text states this quantification result from ECIA experiments shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The Lar-Sns binding signal is about twofold weaker than the Sns-Kirre binding signal.
source: The binding signal is about twofold weaker than that obtained for the strong binding partners Sns and Kirre, which bind to each other with a Kd of 2.5 µM (Ozkan et al., 2014).
evidence: The text compares the binding signals and cites a previous study for the Sns-Kirre Kd value.

claim: Hbs and Kirre do not bind to Lar.
source: We also tested whether Hbs and Kirre, the other members of the IRM protein family, also bind to Lar. No binding was observed for either Hbs-AP5 or Kirre-AP5, while Kirre-Fc and Hbs-AP5 showed strong binding, as previously observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Ozkan et al., 2014).
evidence: The text states no binding was observed, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows the ECIA results.

claim: PTPRF-AP5 staining intensity increased 18- to 20-fold in Tub>NPHS1 and Tub>Sns embryos relative to wild-type.
source: Staining intensity was increased by 18- to 20-fold relative to WT when Nephrin or Sns were expressed (Figure 1L).
evidence: The text states this quantification result, which is shown in Figure 1L.

claim: PTPRD-AP5 staining in the VNC increased threefold when Nephrin was ectopically expressed.
source: When Nephrin was ectopically expressed using Tub-GAL4 (Tub>NPHS1), midline glial staining was slightly increased in intensity, and there was a threefold increase in staining relative to WT in the VNC as a whole (Figure 1M–O).
evidence: The text states this quantification result, which is shown in Figure 1O.

claim: PTPRF and PTPRD bind to fly Sns in vitro.
source: We then tested PTPRF and PTPRD for binding to Sns and Nephrin in vitro. Fc dimers for both human proteins bound to fly Sns-AP5 (Figure 1Q).
evidence: The text states this result, which is shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: PTPRF-AP5 binds to Nephrin-Fc in vitro.
source: PTPRF-AP5 also bound to Nephrin-Fc, and there was a smaller (but still significant) increase over background for Nephrin and PTPRD-AP5 (Figure 1Q).
evidence: The text states this result, which is shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: The Lar-Sns interaction is evolutionarily conserved for at least two of the three mammalian Lar orthologs.
source: In summary, these data indicate that the Lar–Sns interaction is evolutionarily conserved for at least two of the three mammalian Lar orthologs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the binding data shown in Figure 1I-Q.

claim: Lar-T2A-GAL4 is expressed in motor neurons and interneurons in the third instar larval VNC.
source: In the third instar larval VNC, Lar-T2A-GAL4>UAS-EGFP (Lar>GFP) expression was observed in motor neurons (large paired cells) and in a large number of interneurons (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Sns-T2A-GAL4 is expressed in motor neurons in the third instar larval VNC.
source: Sns-T2A-GAL4>UAS-EGFP (Sns>GFP) expression was also seen in motor neurons (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as in a pattern of interneurons that appeared different from those expressing the Lar reporter (Figure 2D).
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lar>GFP is expressed in both 1b and 1s glutamatergic motor neurons but not in modulatory type II or type III motor neurons.
source: Examination of NMJs showed that Lar>GFP was expressed in both types of glutamatergic motor neurons (1b and 1s) (Figure 2K), but not in modulatory type II or type III motor neurons (Figure 2E and E').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figures 2E, E', and K.

claim: Lar>GFP expression is stronger in 1s than in 1b motor neurons.
source: Lar>GFP expression was stronger in 1s than in 1b motor neurons (Figure 2G and G').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 2G and G'.

claim: Sns>GFP is expressed in both 1b and 1s motor neurons with stronger expression in 1s neurons.
source: Sns>GFP was also expressed in both 1b and 1s motor neurons with stronger expression in 1s neurons (Figure 2H, H' and L).
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figures 2H, H', and L.

claim: Sns>GFP is expressed in type II motor neurons.
source: Sns>GFP was also observed in type II motor neurons (Figure 2F and F').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 2F and F'.

claim: No Sns>GFP or Lar>GFP expression was seen in muscles.
source: No Sns>GFP or Lar>GFP expression was seen in muscles.
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation.

claim: Lar13.2/snsxb3 and Lar451/snsxb3 transheterozygotes have strong NMJ phenotypes similar to Lar null animals.
source: Lar/+ and sns/+ heterozygote controls had no 7/6 NMJ phenotypes, but the two Lar/sns transhets had strong phenotypes, similar to Lar null animals (Lar13.2/Lar451) (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: The text describes the phenotypes shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: Lar13.2/snsxb3 and Lar451/snsxb3 transheterozygote NMJs show severe reduction in NMJ area, number of boutons, total NMJ length, longest branch length, and number of 1b branches.
source: Both Lar13.2/snsxb3 and Lar451/snsxb3 transhet NMJs showed severe reduction in NMJ area, number of boutons, total NMJ length, longest branch length, and number of 1b branches (Figure 3G–K).
evidence: The text describes the quantified phenotypes shown in Figure 3G-K.

claim: There is no significant difference between Lar451/snsxb3 transheterozygotes and Lar13.2/Lar451 mutants for any of the NMJ parameters measured.
source: There was no significant difference between the stronger Lar451/snsxb3 transhet and Lar13.2/Lar451 mutants for any of the NMJ parameters measured, indicating that Lar and Sns probably function in the same genetic pathway.
evidence: The text states this result and draws an inference about genetic pathway interaction.

claim: The 1s NMJ on muscle 7/6 is similarly affected in Lar/Sns transheterozygotes as the 1b NMJ.
source: The 1s NMJ on muscle 7/6 is similarly affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this result, which is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Lar-Sns interaction is not required for the role of Sns in myoblast fusion during embryonic development.
source: There was no difference in the size or shape of muscles in the transhets or the Lar mutants. This suggests that the Lar–Sns interaction is not required for the role of Sns in myoblast fusion during embryonic development.
evidence: The text states this observation and draws an inference.

claim: Lar451/snsxb3 transheterozygotes and Lar13.2/Lar451 mutants have 64% and 71% fewer Brp punctae per 7/6 NMJ than wild-type, respectively.
source: Lar451/snsxb3 transhets and Lar13.2/Lar451 mutants had 64 and 71% fewer Brp punctae per 7/6 NMJ than WT (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: The text states this quantification result, which is shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: There is no compensatory increase in the number of synaptic active zones in response to reduced NMJ size and number of boutons in Lar/Sns transheterozygotes.
source: This indicates that there is no compensatory increase in the number of synaptic active zones in response to reduced NMJ size and number of boutons.
evidence: The text draws this inference from the Brp punctae data.

claim: Neuronal knockdown of Lar or Sns causes NMJ abnormalities similar to those seen in Lar/sns transheterozygotes and Lar mutants.
source: Neuronal knockdown of Lar or Sns caused NMJ abnormalities similar to those seen in Lar/sns transhets and Lar mutants (Figure 3N–S).
evidence: The text describes the RNAi results shown in Figure 3N-S.

claim: The 7/6 NMJ phenotypes of Lar/sns transheterozygotes are likely due to a reduction in interactions between Lar and Sns in the same neuron (in cis).
source: The RP3 and MNISNb/d-1s axons, which form the 1b and 1s arbors of the muscle 7/6 NMJ, do not contact other motor or sensory axons after leaving the ISNb bundle, and the 1b and 1s portions of the 7/6 NMJ are separate from each other. Thus, it is likely that the 7/6 NMJ phenotypes of Lar/sns transhets are due to a reduction in interactions between Lar and Sns in the same neuron (in cis).
evidence: The text provides anatomical reasoning to support this inference.

claim: Reducing Sns levels with neuronal sns RNAi in a Lar mutant background does not increase the severity of the 1b NMJ phenotypes.
source: Reducing Sns levels with neuronal sns RNAi in this Lar mutant background did not increase the severity of the 1b NMJ phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), further confirming that Lar and Sns interact in the same genetic pathway.
evidence: The text states this result and draws an inference, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neuronal kirre RNAi does not have any effect on 1b NMJs.
source: Moreover, neuronal kirre RNAi did not have any effect on 1b NMJs, indicating that the Sns-Kirre interaction, which plays a role in embryonic myoblast fusion and nephrocyte development, may not be involved in NMJ development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this result and draws an inference, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lar is expressed in Kenyon cells (KCs) of the larval mushroom body.
source: Lar was found to be expressed in Kenyon cells (KCs), the principal cells of the MB, using antibody staining. Here, we confirmed that Lar is expressed in larval KCs using Lar>GFP (Figure 4A–B').
evidence: The text states this result, which is shown in Figure 4A-B', and cites previous antibody staining work.

claim: Lar>GFP labels both the dorsal (d) and the medial (m) lobes of the larval MB.
source: A single optical slice shows that Lar>GFP labels both the dorsal (d) and the medial (m) lobes of the larval MB (Figure 4C').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 4C'.

claim: There is no Sns>GFP expression in KCs of the larval mushroom body.
source: Sns>GFP was not detected in KCs (Figure 4D), but was seen in many other neurons in the larval central brain.
evidence: The text states this observation, which is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No Sns reporter expression could be seen in either the dorsal or medial lobes of the larval MB.
source: No Sns reporter expression could be seen in either the dorsal or medial lobes of the MB (Figure 4E and E').
evidence: The text states this observation, which is shown in Figure 4E and E'.

claim: Sns-expressing neurons have dendritic projections enveloping the dorsal lobes of the MB.
source: In order to determine if Sns is expressed in neurons postsynaptic to MB axons, we used a dendrite-specific marker (UAS-Drep2) (Andlauer et al., 2014) to label Sns-expressing neurons. We observed Drep2-expressing neurons enveloping the dorsal lobes of the MB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that Sns-expressing neurons are postsynaptic to Lar-expressing KCs.
evidence: The text describes this result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and cites the Drep2 marker reference.

claim: Sns does not co-localize with Repo-positive glial cells.
source: We also performed immunostaining using Sns>GFP and anti-Repo to label glial cells, but did not see any co-localization between GFP and Repo (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this observation, which is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lar mutants have medial lobe axons that fail to stop at the midline and instead cross over to the contralateral side, forming a fused medial lobe.
source: Lar mutants have two distinct phenotypes in the larval MB. First, the medial lobe axons fail to stop at the midline, instead crossing over to the contralateral side and forming a fused medial lobe.
evidence: The text describes this phenotype and cites a previous study (Kurusu and Zinn, 2008).

claim: Lar mutants have KC axons that do not branch properly or dorsal branches do not extend after branching, resulting in reduced or absent dorsal lobes.
source: Second, KC axons do not branch properly (or dorsal branches do not extend after branching), resulting in reduced or absent dorsal lobes (Kurusu and Zinn, 2008).
evidence: The text describes this phenotype and cites a previous study.

claim: Lar13.2/snsxb3 and Lar451/snsxb3 transheterozygotes display fused medial lobes, similar to Lar13.2/Lar451 mutants.
source: However, both Lar13.2/snsxb3 and Lar451/snsxb3 transhets as well as Lar13.2/snsDf transhets displayed fused medial lobes, similar to Lar13.2/Lar451 mutants (Figure 4I–L, M and M', Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text describes the phenotypes shown in Figures 4I-L, M, M' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dorsal lobe phenotypes are observed in Lar mutants and Lar/sns transheterozygotes, with most dorsal lobes being absent in Lar13.2/Lar451 and Lar451/snsxb3.
source: We also observed dorsal lobe phenotypes in Lar mutants and Lar/sns transhets, with most dorsal lobes being absent in Lar13.2/Lar451 and Lar451/snsxb3 (Figure 4I, K, L, N and N').
evidence: The text describes the phenotypes shown in Figures 4I, K, L, N, and N'.

claim: There is no strong correlation between medial lobe fusion and dorsal lobe phenotypes in individual animals.
source: We did not observe a strong correlation between the two phenotypes; an animal with a fused medial lobe did not always display reduced or absent dorsal lobes.
evidence: The text states this observation.

claim: Pan-neuronal RNAi knockdown of Lar and Sns results in medial lobe fusion and loss of dorsal lobes.
source: Similar to our genetic analyses, we found that knocking down Sns and Lar resulted in medial lobe fusion and loss of dorsal lobes.
evidence: The text describes the RNAi results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lar and Sns act in trans in the larval MB.
source: These data show that Lar interacts with Sns to regulate the formation of the larval MB. The Lar-Sns interaction in this context is likely to be in trans as we do not observe any Sns>GFP expression in larval KCs or in the MB lobes.
evidence: The text draws this inference from the expression data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: Lar RNAi knockdown in all MB neurons results in medial lobe fusion in the larval MB.
source: Lar RNAi knockdown in all MB neurons resulted in medial lobe fusion in the larval MB, confirming that Lar acts in MB neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text describes this result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MB-specific Sns RNAi knockdown does not cause any abnormalities in the larval MB.
source: MB-specific Sns RNAi knockdown, however, did not cause any abnormalities in the larval MB.
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combining a Lar heterozygote (Lar13.2/+) with MB-specific sns RNAi does not cause any MB phenotypes.
source: Combining a Lar heterozygote (Lar13.2/+) with MB-specific sns RNAi also did not cause any MB phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neuronal kirre RNAi does not have any effect on the larval MB.
source: Neuronal kirre RNAi did not have any effect on the larval MB (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 24 hr APF, Lar>GFP expression is detectable on growth cones of α/β KC axons near the midline in the β lobes.
source: At 24 hr after puparium formation (APF), Lar>GFP expression was detectable on growth cones of α/β KC axons near the midline in the β lobes (Figure 5A–B', arrows).
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 5A-B'.

claim: At 40 hr APF, higher levels of Lar>GFP expression are seen in both α/β lobes as well as α′/β′ lobes.
source: At 40 hr APF, higher levels of Lar>GFP expression were seen in both α/β lobes as well as α′/β′ lobes.
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 5E-F'.

claim: Lar expression peaks at 72 hr APF, with strong expression in all lobes.
source: Lar expression peaks at 72 hr APF, with strong expression in all lobes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B'.

claim: Lar is expressed in α/β lobes, but not in α′/β′ lobes, in the adult MB.
source: Lar is also expressed in α/β lobes, but not in α′/β′ lobes, in the adult MB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-H'.

claim: No Sns>GFP expression is detected in either the α/β lobes or the α′/β′ lobes in the 24 hr APF and 40 hr APF MB.
source: However, we did not observe any detectable Sns>GFP expression in either the α/β lobes or the α′/β′ lobes in the 24 hr APF and 40 hr APF MB (Figure 5C–D' and G–H').
evidence: The text states this observation shown in Figures 5C-D' and G-H'.

claim: There is weak Sns>GFP expression in α/β lobes at 72 hr APF.
source: There is weak Sns>GFP expression in α/β lobes at 72 hr APF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D'), but lobes with a mature morphology have already formed by this time, so this is not relevant to the lobe phenotypes we observe.
evidence: The text describes this observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D' and draws an inference.

claim: Sns>GFP is weakly expressed in adult α/β lobes.
source: Sns>GFP is also weakly expressed in adult α/β lobes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J',K–L').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I-J', K-L'.

claim: Sns>GFP and Lar>GFP label specific glomeruli in the antennal lobes at 40 hr APF and 72 hr APF.
source: We observed Sns>GFP and Lar>GFP labeling of specific glomeruli at 40 hr APF and 72 hr APF (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lar13.2/Snsxb3, Lar451/Snsxb3, and Lar13.2/Lar451 animals show 75%, 79%, and 93% missing α lobes, respectively.
source: Lar13.2/Snsxb3, Lar451/Snsxb3, and Lar13.2/Lar451 animals showed 75, 79, and 93% missing α lobes, respectively.
evidence: The text states these quantification results shown in Figure 6H and H'.

claim: Lar/sns transheterozygotes and Lar mutants display midline crossing of β lobe axons, creating a fused β lobe.
source: Lar/sns transhets and Lar mutants also displayed midline crossing of β lobe axons, with most β lobe axons crossing the midline, creating a fused β lobe, instead of two separate lobes (Figure 6D–H').
evidence: The text describes the phenotypes shown in Figure 6D-H'.

claim: The thickness of fused β lobes in Lar/sns transheterozygotes and Lar mutants is significantly greater than normal unfused β lobes in control animals.
source: The thickness of these fused β lobes was significantly greater than the normal unfused β lobes seen in control animals.
evidence: The text states this observation.

claim: Most Lar/sns transheterozygote and Lar null animals are missing one or more α′ lobes.
source: Most Lar/sns transhet and Lar null animals were missing one or more α′ lobes (Figure 6L–N, P and P').
evidence: The text describes the phenotypes shown in Figure 6L-N, P, and P'.

claim: β′ lobes display midline crossing, resulting in a single fused β′ lobe in most or all Lar/sns transheterozygotes and Lar null animals.
source: β′ lobes displayed midline crossing, resulting in a single fused β′ lobe in most or all Lar/sns transhets and Lar null animals (Figure 6L–N, O and O').
evidence: The text describes the phenotypes shown in Figure 6L-N, O, and O'.

claim: The Lar, sns, and Lar/sns phenotypes are more penetrant in β′ lobes than in β lobes.
source: Thus, the Lar, sns, and Lar/sns phenotypes were even stronger in β′ lobes than in β lobes.
evidence: The text draws this inference from the quantification data in Figure 6.

claim: γ lobes in all animals are normal and show no phenotype in either Lar/sns transheterozygotes or Lar nulls.
source: Interestingly, γ lobes in all animals were normal and showed no phenotype in either Lar/sns transhets or Lar nulls (Figure 6I–N).
evidence: The text states this observation shown in Figure 6I-N.

claim: γ KC axons do not require Lar or Sns for midline stopping.
source: γ KC axons re-extend during the pupal phase, and they apparently do not require Lar or Sns for midline stopping.
evidence: The text draws this inference from the lack of γ lobe phenotypes.

claim: MB-specific Lar RNAi results in β′ lobe fusion in 75% of animals.
source: MB-specific Lar RNAi resulted in β′ lobe fusion in 75% animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: sns RNAi in MB neurons does not cause any MB phenotypes, either alone or in combination with a Lar heterozygote.
source: sns RNAi in MB neurons did not cause any MB phenotypes, either alone or in combination with a Lar heterozygote (Lar13.2/+) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Lar and Sns act in trans in the adult MB as well.
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and draws an inference.

claim: Pan-neuronal sns RNAi causes β′ lobe fusion in ~50% of animals.
source: Pan-neuronal sns RNAi caused β′ lobe fusion in ~50% animals, while kirre RNAi had no effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pan-neuronal kirre RNAi has no effect on β′ lobe fusion.
source: Pan-neuronal sns RNAi caused β′ lobe fusion in ~50% animals, while kirre RNAi had no effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lar>GFP is strongly expressed at both 40 and 72 hr APF in L1 lamina neuron cell bodies.
source: We observed strong Lar>GFP expression at both 40 and 72 hr APF in L1 lamina neuron cell bodies (Figure 7C–C' and G–G').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 7C-C' and G-G'.

claim: Lar>GFP is expressed at high levels in M1 and M5 layers of the medulla where L1 neurons arborize.
source: Lar>GFP was also expressed at high levels in M1 and M5 layers of the medulla where L1 neurons arborize (Figure 7D–D' and H–H').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 7D-D' and H-H'.

claim: Lar is expressed at very high levels in pupal L1 and at low levels in R7 according to sequencing of pupal lamina neuron mRNA.
source: This is consistent with results of sequencing of pupal lamina neuron mRNA, which showed that Lar is expressed at very high levels in pupal L1 and at low levels in R7 (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: The text cites a previous RNA sequencing study.

claim: Lar>GFP is expressed in photoreceptor cell bodies in the 24 hr APF retina.
source: Lar>GFP is expressed in photoreceptor cell bodies in the 24 hr APF retina (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and B'.

claim: Stronger Lar>GFP expression is seen in R7 and/or R8 photoreceptors, which lie in the center of each ommatidium.
source: Stronger expression was seen in R7 and/or R8 photoreceptors, which lie in the center of each ommatidium.
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and B'.

claim: There is no Lar>GFP expression in adult photoreceptors.
source: There was no Lar>GFP expression in adult photoreceptors.
evidence: The text states this observation.

claim: Many neurons express Sns>GFP in the 40 and 72 hr APF medullary cortex.
source: Many neurons expressed Sns>GFP in the 40 and 72 hr APF medullary cortex (Figure 7E–E'' and I–I'').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 7E-E'' and I-I''.

claim: By 72 hr APF, Sns expression can be seen in dots at the top of the lamina, which are likely to be C2 endings.
source: By 72 hr APF, Sns expression could be seen in dots at the top of the lamina, which are likely to be C2 endings (Figure 7I'), as well as in M1 and M5 layers of the medulla (Figure 7J and J').
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern shown in Figure 7I', J, and J' and draws an inference.

claim: The Sns expression pattern in the lamina and M1, M5, and M10 layers of the medulla matches the arborization pattern of C2 neurons.
source: This matches the arborization pattern of C2 neurons, which are synaptic partners of L1 neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F'').
evidence: The text draws this inference and shows the comparison in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E-F''.

claim: C2 neurons are the only neurons with a dot-like pattern of endings, one at the top of each lamina cartridge.
source: C2 neurons are the only neurons with this dot-like pattern of endings, one at the top of each lamina cartridge (see Tuthill et al., 2013).
evidence: The text cites a previous study characterizing C2 morphology.

claim: Sns>GFP is not detected in photoreceptors at any pupal stage.
source: We did not detect Sns>GFP expression in photoreceptors at any pupal stage.
evidence: The text states this observation.

claim: The pupal and adult Sns>GFP pattern appears identical to the pattern observed with a C2-specific split-GAL4 driver.
source: The pupal and adult Sns>GFP pattern appeared identical to the pattern observed with a C2-specific split-GAL4 driver (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F'').
evidence: The text draws this inference from the comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-F''.

claim: Sns expression in lamina and the M1 and M5 layers of the medulla at least partly represents postsynaptic elements.
source: We used Drep2 to label dendrites of Sns-T2A-GAL4-expressing neurons in the adult OL and found that the Sns expression seen in lamina and the M1 and M5 layers of the medulla at least partly represents postsynaptic elements (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and A').
evidence: The text describes this result shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and A'.

claim: C2 neurons are bidirectionally connected to L1 neurons in M1 and M5.
